title: Sirhind, 1710
hookLine: Banda's forces take Sirhind, and land is given to those who till it

lines: LAND A FAMILY HAS WORKED FOR GENERATIONS.
A LANDLORD WHO NEVER TOUCHED IT.
THE LAND BELONGS TO THOSE WHO WORK IT.
cards: A farmer plows land his family has worked for generations. He plants it, brings in the harvest, then watches a large share go to a landlord who has never touched the soil, and another share go in taxes.
What's left barely feeds his children. Then a rider comes to the village with news: the land now belongs to the people who work it. For many Punjabi farmers in 1710, something like that happened.
It began at a city with a painful name in Sikh memory. Today: Sirhind.

teach.h: SIRHIND — WHERE THE YOUNG SONS DIED.
teach.b: Sirhind was a rich Mughal city on the road between Delhi and Lahore, governed by Wazir Khan.

A few years earlier, it was in Sirhind, under his authority, that Guru Gobind Singh's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were executed. They were small boys. Sikhs everywhere knew that name.
When Banda Singh Bahadur arrived in Punjab with the Guru's arrows and letters, thousands joined him, many of them poor farmers.

In May 1710, at a place called Chappar Chiri, his forces met Wazir Khan's army. Wazir Khan was killed, and the Sikhs took Sirhind. Historians record that the city was sacked, and that many of its people suffered.
That's part of the honest story too. Then Banda did something that made him remembered far beyond the battlefield.
He set up his own rule, with a fort called Lohgarh, and struck coins in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, not his own.

teach.h: THE LAND TO THOSE WHO TILL IT.
teach.b: And in the lands he held, he broke the power of the big landlords, the zamindars, and let the land go to those who actually tilled it. How complete that change was, and how long it lasted, historians still debate.
But for farmers in Banda's lands, for a time, the soil under their feet was their own.
Today a great gurdwara, Fatehgarh Sahib, stands at Sirhind where the young sons died. Every December, Sikhs go there in their thousands to remember them.
Victory at Sirhind is remembered with that grief, not instead of it.

how: Each December, Sikhs gather in large numbers at Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib near Sirhind for the Shaheedi Jor Mela, remembering the martyrdom of Guru Gobind Singh's youngest sons; Banda's victory of 1710 is remembered alongside it.

games.q: you're Banda. you've taken Sirhind. the farmers who joined you work land owned by big landlords. what do you do?

games.why: Banda broke the zamindars' power where he ruled and let the tillers have the land, though historians debate how far it went.

practice: Think about what you have plenty of, not necessarily money: time on a weekend, books you've read, clothes you don't wear, a skill someone else is struggling with, a spare room, a patient ear.
Picture someone who works hard for something you have more of than you need. Choose one thing you could share, and the person you'd share it with.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Sirhind (also written Sarhind), the Mughal city between Delhi and Lahore.
